unfortunately, people settle for SUPPRESSING that 'passion' so people think it's the fault of the material or the authors when really it's the fault of the teachers.
I picked up a passion for reading from school. It gave me something to do in spite of all the crap that was being taught.

I think there's too much anti-learning bravado from idiots in schools to allow creative passions to be nurtured. These children should be burned, along with their parents, or sent to a morons building where they can learn to separate recycled rubbish, so we can build a better society :)

If anything I found reading at school put me off particular authors - putting aside the stuff I still think is complete crap or just not my cup of tea - the only thing that got me into reading was my parents reading to me and shoving books in my face as a small child.

The issue is general genres. Sure, there's plenty of people who enjoy a wide variety but if you want to get somebody into the medium, you need to show them something they'd enjoy (no school is going to assign reading The Hunt For Red October, for example) and you can't work that into set English exam. By the age of high school, the only real way they'll get into reading is if they do it themselves - you can't force it.

It starts with being read to at home. Sometimes, that's enough, especially if the book choice fits the child and the reader puts effort into it. After that, it's about role modeling. Maybe it's true you can't teach passion, but as a teacher I tried to spark and nurture it. Feedback from students and their families was generally supportive.
